# Semantic rename integration fixtures

These projects exercise real indexing and the public `rename` tool in both modes
(`dry_run: true` to preview, `dry_run: false` to apply). The integration test and its
subprocess helper do not mock the parser, semantic resolver, registry, database,
graph, filesystem, or rename functions.

Run from `gitnexus/`:

```sh
npm run build
npm test -- test/integration/rename-provider-matrix
```

Four test files partition the sorted cases evenly so CI can distribute real
indexing across its existing shards. Each case runs exactly once.

Use `-t 'cpp/'` (for example) to select one provider. Rebuild after production
changes: the helper loads the built application, including real parse workers.
Do not rebuild while this suite is running. The analyzer verifies that its build
does not change during indexing.

Each case contains a `case.json`, an independently authored `before/` project,
and the complete expected `after/` project. Unchanged files are included too.
Expected files are never generated by applying the implementation's edits.

For each case, the harness:

1. Copies the project into an isolated temporary repository and creates a real
   index, registry entry, and database with PDG enabled.
2. Checks indexing completeness and selects the target uniquely from persisted
   declarations. It asserts the specified call, access, or family edges.
3. Calls `rename` with `dry_run: true` and verifies that all source bytes are unchanged.
4. Calls `rename` with `dry_run: false`, checks the exact edit count and agreement
   with the preview, and compares every source file against `after/`.
5. Reindexes successful edits and checks the renamed declaration and the same
   graph relationships at their source positions.

Refusal cases assert their specific error and planning status and verify that
both preview and apply preserve every source byte. They supplement successful
cases; the suite requires successful fixtures for every supported language.

`target` and edge endpoints use `name`, `file`, optional `kind`, and optional
zero-based `startLine`. Add `startLine` when declarations share a name. An optional
`expectedTargetName` records an escaped graph spelling after rename, such as
`@Serialize`; the generic harness contains no language-specific name rules.

An optional `exactOutgoing: true` requires every listed source/type pair to have
exactly the target set specified in `edges`, rejecting extra overload or wrong-owner
edges. This applies to cold, warm-cache, and post-rename graphs.

An optional `warmParseCache: true` performs a second forced index before rename,
using captures cached by the cold index. It requires cache hits, zero reparsed
files and no parse workers, then verifies the same persisted target identity and
specified graph edges before public preview/apply. The C++ overload fixture uses
this path to preserve signature-specific call edges across cache serialization.

| Provider    | Language behavior exercised                                                                        |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| C           | Header/definition families, function pointers, call chains, deep pointer fields                    |
| C++         | Overloaded free functions across headers, virtual families, deep pointer fields, language keywords |
| C#          | Interface/override families, public fields, escaped overloads, named arguments                     |
| COBOL       | Cross-program calls, paragraph chains, nested qualified data                                       |
| Dart        | Interface/override and super calls, deep fields, imports, contextual identifiers                   |
| Go          | Structural interfaces, exported pointer fields, package import aliases, generic type shadowing     |
| Java        | Interface/override families, overloads, deep public fields, reserved names                         |
| JavaScript  | Inheritance, inferred deep fields, escaped exports, aliases and shorthand                          |
| Kotlin      | Override families, typed callable references, escaped overloads, property writes                   |
| Objective-C | Protocol selectors, accessors, deep chains, ivars and same-named C symbols                         |
| PHP         | Case-insensitive methods/functions, case-sensitive properties, grouped imports                     |
| Python      | Override families, deep fields, aliases, Unicode names, dynamic attribute safety                   |
| Ruby        | Mixins, predicate methods, chained setters, required qualified constants                           |
| Rust        | Trait families, borrowed field receivers, cross-file import aliases                                |
| Swift       | Protocol/override families, deep properties, escaped names and argument labels                     |
| TypeScript  | Constructor-proven families/chains, aliases/shorthand, structural safety refusals                  |
| Vue         | Script/template/CSS references, components, cross-file calls, opaque raw blocks                    |
| Zig         | Typed container fields, import aliases and call chains                                             |

C, COBOL and Zig do not have class polymorphism matching the OO cases. Their
fixtures exercise their own callable, program, or container semantics. Vue
fixtures additionally cover its embedded and template name surfaces.

TypeScript's structurally typed parameters do not prove a receiver's constructor:
unrelated objects can satisfy the same annotation. Open-parameter refusal cases
remain unchanged, alongside successful constructor-proven cases. These fixtures
are targeted regression coverage, not a claim of complete IDE refactoring parity.

C++ permits `restrict` as an identifier ([C++ keyword table](https://eel.is/c++draft/lex.key),
[GCC's explicit clarification](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Restricted-Pointers.html)).
The successful type fixture exercises this spelling. The vendored tree-sitter
grammar currently parses an unparenthesized `int restrict(...)` declarator as a
C-style type qualifier, so the separate function fixture expects `parse_error`
and unchanged sources. The parser limitation remains fail-closed.
